overview: About 280 teeth, jaws and ankle bones document an early Eocene carnivoraform sample and replace the historical two-tooth picture of “Miacis” latouri.

ecology.diet: Small-prey or insectivorous diet inferred from dentition
ecology.habitat: Warm early Eocene woodland inferred from locality context
ecology.locomotion: Arboreal capability inferred from tarsal anatomy
ecology.bodySize: Small carnivoraform represented by dental and tarsal material
ecology.guild: Small scansorial faunivore inferred from anatomy

traits: Reconstructed permanent dentition
Astragali and calcaneum
Character-matrix placement among basal carnivoraforms
evidenceSummary: The catalogued sample supports dental, tarsal and matrix claims but does not demonstrate crown Carnivora, a direct ancestor or the global first carnivoramorphan.

commonNameZh: 西藏化石豹亚科（原始归属）
overview: A partial cranium and associated jaw material entered a combined fossil–molecular analysis; the original Panthera and snow-leopard affinity remain revisable analytical assignments.

ecology.habitat: High-elevation Zanda Basin palaeoenvironment inferred independently
ecology.locomotion: Not preserved by the cranial sample
ecology.bodySize: Pantherine size inferred from partial cranial material
ecology.guild: Large terrestrial carnivore inferred from dentition

traits: Adult partial cranium
Associated ramus and premaxilla fragments
Characters used in a combined total-evidence analysis
evidenceSummary: IVPP V18788.1–3 and the original magnetostratigraphic framework are explicit; taxonomic assignment, affinity and Asian biogeographic scenario remain open to revision.

overview: Holotype NUFV 405 preserves about 65% of one skeleton, combining terrestrial limb proportions with traits used to infer freshwater swimming.

ecology.habitat: Freshwater lake setting; habitual habitat inferred
ecology.locomotion: Terrestrial and semiaquatic capability inferred from limb and body proportions

traits: Substantial skull and postcranial skeleton
Weight-bearing limbs with swimming-related proportions
Long tail and freshwater depositional context
evidenceSummary: The associated skeleton supports an anatomical mosaic, while semiaquatic locomotion, pinnipedimorph placement and a freshwater transition are interpretations rather than an ancestor sequence.

geography: North American Hesperocyoninae localities sampled by Wang
overview: Wang's monograph revises Hesperocyon within the extinct hesperocyonine canid radiation using named fossil material and a morphology matrix; its sampled placement is not presented as direct ancestry to later canids.

ecology.diet: Not resolved by the monograph as a directly observed diet
ecology.habitat: Not resolved as a genus-wide habitat by the sampled systematics
ecology.locomotion: Postcranial locomotor performance is not established by the cited monograph
ecology.bodySize: No genus-wide body-size estimate is projected from the sampled material
ecology.guild: No single ecological guild is assigned from the cited systematic evidence

traits: Named Hesperocyon specimens revised in a fossil canid monograph
Dental and cranial characters scored in a morphology matrix
Species-level relationships tested within sampled Hesperocyoninae
evidenceSummary: The primary monograph directly supports the named fossil and matrix sample. Its 40–29 Ma display is only a source-bounded sampled-genus window, while placement, ecology and ancestry remain qualified.

geography: Pyramid Hill Sandstone Member, Jewett Sand
overview: LACM 4321 is a virtually complete Enaliarctos mealsi skeleton from the Pyramid Hill Sandstone Member of the Jewett Sand, used for bounded comparisons of axial and limb locomotor capability rather than a direct pinniped-ancestor claim.

ecology.diet: Not resolved by the cited skeletal locomotor study
ecology.habitat: Jewett Sand depositional setting; habitual ecology is not directly observed
ecology.locomotion: Aquatic and terrestrial locomotor capacities inferred comparatively from axial and limb anatomy
ecology.bodySize: Not projected as a genus-wide body-size estimate from one skeleton
ecology.guild: No feeding guild is assigned from the cited skeletal evidence

traits: Virtually complete LACM 4321 skeleton
Flexible lumbar vertebral morphology in the comparative interpretation
Flipper-like limbs with developed bony processes and muscle-attachment areas
evidenceSummary: The skeleton, member and central-California occurrence are direct records. Monophyly, ursid relationship, swimming strokes and terrestrial performance remain the primary study's comparative inferences, not a universal pinniped history.

overview: Named craniodental and postcranial material from southern California was tested in morphology matrices; the broad analysis leaves nearby carnivoramorphan relationships unresolved, while a Paleogene-only subset recovers a caniform position outside crown Canoidea.

ecology.diet: Carnivory is a discriminant-model prediction, not observed feeding
ecology.habitat: Santiago Formation member C depositional context; habitual habitat is not directly observed
ecology.locomotion: Postcranial elements are preserved, but locomotor performance is not established
ecology.bodySize: About 6 kg estimated for the holotype by a tooth-based regression
ecology.guild: No ecological guild is assigned beyond the comparative dietary model

traits: UCMP 85202 cranium and dentition
SDSNH associated cranial, mandibular and postcranial material
Associated postcranial elements documented with the craniodental sample
evidenceSummary: The profile is bounded to named southern-California specimens and a source-level occurrence window. Its caniform placement and dietary classification are matrix and comparative-model results, not direct ancestry, a global range, or observed behaviour.

overview: A left P4, right M1 and partial mandible from two Spanish middle Miocene localities were analysed in a fossil-plus-living ursid matrix that recovers the sampled genus within Ailuropodinae.

ecology.diet: Dental comparisons suggest a more herbivorous tendency; feeding was not observed
ecology.habitat: Spanish locality records only; habitual habitat is not directly observed
ecology.locomotion: Not resolved by the cited dental and mandibular material
ecology.bodySize: Small-sized ailuropodine in the published diagnosis; no population estimate is projected
ecology.guild: No ecological guild is assigned from the available dental sample

traits: Holotype left P4 MNCN-CSIC NV-2-42
Paratype right M1 NV-2-40 and partial mandible IPS 46473
Published dental and mandibular morphology documented from the named specimens
evidenceSummary: Named Spanish dental specimens and localities are direct records. Ailuropodine placement and dietary tendency are published comparative results; they do not establish direct ancestry, identical giant-panda ecology, a secure origin centre, or a global first appearance.
